full_judgment:
Is the Civil Court so powerless that in exercise of its inherent powers it cannot entertain an application for setting aside an ex parte decree which is alleged to have been obtained on practicing fraud upon the court itself? This is the question for decision before me. The problem arises thus; in August, 1973 one Sk. AM Ershad, the predecessor of the opposite parties, brought a suit being Title Suit No. 90 of 1973 for specific performance of a contract for sale of 13 kathas of land including a two storied building at 3, New Bailey Road, Dhaka on the allegations that petitioner No. 1 being the owner of the holding executed an agreement dated 15.8.71 for sale of the same to him at a consideration of Tk. 1,00,000.00 and that in pursuance thereof she also put the plaintiff in possession of the ground floor of the building on 3.8.72. Petitioner No. 1 and her husband, petitioner No. 2 were arrayed as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the suit. They denied the alleged contract. A Subordinate Judge of Dhaka after the hearing dismissed the suit. The plaintiff took an appeal being FA No. 19 of 1978 there from to this Court. During the pendency of the appeal he died and the opposite parties got themselves substituted in his place as heirs and legal representatives. They prosecuted the appeal. A Division Bench of this Court upheld the decision of the trial court on the findings, inter alia: 

 4. After a lapse of about 4 and half months the said plaintiffs filed another suit being Title Suit No. 183 of 1986 in the 4th Court of Munsif, now Assistant Judge, Dhaka in respect of the self-same property. This time an injunctive relief was sought for against the same set of defendants on the averment that they acquired title to the entire property by adverse possession. The suit was decreed ex parte on 9.7.87. 

 5. An application purporting to be one under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was subsequently made by the defendants for setting aside the decree on the ground of fraud committed on the Court. They alleged that there was willful concealment of material facts in the plaint and fraudulent suppression of the summons to mislead the court. 

 8. The fact that there was other remedies available to the defendants for setting aside the decree is not disputed. It is also not in dispute that as a general rule the powers of the Court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not to be invoked where there is specific provision in the Code which covers a particular case or there is an alternative remedy. It is the contention of the petitioners that the Civil Court has ample reserve of its inherent powers to do what would meet the ends of justice when fraud is committed on the court itself and the learned Assistant Judge has, therefore, committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in refusing to entertain the application for selling aside the ex parte decree. 

 9. Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate who appears for the plaintiffs and opposite parties on the other hand, argues that as there are alternative remedies available to the defendants for setting aside the ex parte decree, it was not open to the learned Assistant Judge to entertain the application in exercise of his inherent powers. He cites several decisions in support. None of these decisions lays down categorically that inherent power of the court can never be exercised for setting aside an ex parte decree or order obtained by fraud practiced upon the court. Strong reliance is placed by the petitioners in Abdul Aziz Vs. Abani Mohan 30 DLR (SC) 221. In that case an order of abatement of an appeal was obtained on production of a false certificate of death. 

 10. In some of the cases referred to in the judgment fraudulent decrees were set aside in exercise of inherent powers of the court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. To the same effect are the decisions in Mofazzal Molla and another Vs. Parul Bala Debi and others 24 DLR 117, Md. Amir Hossain Sarder Vs. Sarat Chandra and others 31 DLR 109, Mozaffar Ahmed & others Vs. Moulvi Saleh Ahmed and others 40 DLR 239. 

 12. It is thus fairly established that in cases of fraud upon the court, the court may exercise its inherent powers to set things right even though there are alternative remedies open. In some of the cases it has been observed that not only the Court has such powers, but it is its duty to set aside the decree or order obtained by fraud practiced upon the court itself when apprised of it.
